title: Winning a pinned piece by attacking it again

card.idea: A pinned piece cannot run away. That is the whole point of it. So you never have to trade for it on its terms: add a second attacker and take it next move instead. The cheapest attacker is a pawn, and a pawn taking a knight wins even when the knight is defended.
card.habit: It cannot run. So do not buy it, attack it again.

explain.text: The bishop on b3 looks straight through the knight on e6 at the king on g8, so the knight is not allowed to move at all. It is attacked once and defended once, by the pawn on d7, so taking it is only a trade. Add a pawn instead: f5.

Now e6 is attacked twice and defended once, and the knight still may not move a square. Black can break the pin by stepping the king aside, but the knight is still standing there when the pawn takes it. A piece for a pawn, and the pawn was free to push.

Here the rook on g1 does the pinning, straight up the open file to the king. The knight on g6 is defended twice, so Rxg6 would cost you the exchange. h5 costs you nothing at all, and a pawn taking a knight does not care how many defenders it has.

challenges.prompt: Tap the black piece that is not allowed to move at all.

hints.text: Look for a line that runs through a black piece and ends on the black king.

challenges.reason: Move the knight on e6 and the bishop on b3 would be hitting the king on g8. That is not a legal move, so the knight stays where it is.

challenges.prompt: White wants to take the pinned knight at once with Bxe6. Is the bishop safe on e6?
reasons: No. The pawn on d7 takes it.
Yes. The knight was pinned, so nothing is allowed to take back.
No. The king on g8 takes it.

hints.text: A pin stops one piece moving. Ask what else is looking at e6.

challenges.reason: A pin stops the knight moving; it does not stop the pawn on d7 recapturing. Bxe6 dxe6 leaves material dead level and the pin gone. The king on g8 is nowhere near e6.

challenges.prompt: The knight on e6 cannot move. Attack it a second time with the cheapest thing you own.

wrong.Bxe6+: dxe6 takes back. You have swapped a bishop for a knight, material is level again, and you gave up the pin to do it.

challenges.reason: f5 costs nothing and makes it two attackers against one defender, on a piece that is not allowed to step out of the way.

challenges.prompt: Why is pushing the pawn better than taking the knight with the bishop?
options: A bishop is worth more than a knight, so the trade loses material.
The pawn attacks the knight for nothing, and the knight still cannot run.
A bishop is not allowed to capture a pinned piece.

hints.text: What do a bishop and a knight cost? And what does pushing a pawn cost?

challenges.reason: A bishop and a knight are both worth three, so taking is only a trade. Pushing the pawn costs nothing, and the knight has nowhere to go.

challenges.prompt: Tap every black man that is defending the knight on g6.

hints.text: Pawns defend the two squares diagonally in front of them. Which two black pawns have g6 in front of them?

challenges.reason: The pawns on f7 and h7. Two defenders, which is exactly why your rook must not take on g6 itself.

challenges.prompt: The knight on g6 is pinned to the king. Bring a second attacker at no cost.

wrong.Rxg6+: hxg6 takes back. You have given a rook for a knight, and the rook was worth far more sitting on g1 holding that knight still.

challenges.reason: h5 attacks the knight a second time for nothing. Because the attacker is a pawn, the two defenders do not matter: hxg6 wins a knight for a pawn.

challenges.prompt: Tap the white piece that is holding the knight on g6 where it stands.

hints.text: Read up the g-file from the bottom of the board and see what is at the top of it.

challenges.reason: The rook on g1 looks up the open g-file at the king on g8. While it sits there, the knight in between is frozen.

takeaway: A pinned piece cannot run, so never trade for it. Bring another attacker, a pawn for choice, and take it next move for nothing.
